first_impression.reaction: My assistant shortlisted it because my father wants a family friend to marry us, and we haven't decided whether the legal part happens in Sydney or wherever the celebration ends up. The first screen is calm and factual, with no gushing, which is fine. It reads like a government explainer with a brand name on the end, though. Her summary for me: a friend can't do it unless they register, which can take months; we check whoever we book on the official register; and an Australian celebrant can't marry us overseas. I read the friend section and the overseas section myself. The four types and the paperwork are hers.

journey.quote: If your celebration is overseas, the answer changes again.
journey.reaction: Good. It tells me early that the part I care about is covered, so my assistant knew where to send me.

journey.quote: The two Commonwealth types share one regulator and one register, which is why they are sometimes grouped as a single type, with three groups in all.
journey.reaction: Four types, then three groups, then 'either way, the same people'. This is the over-explaining I don't need. My assistant skipped it and so did I.

journey.section: Ministers of religion from a recognised denomination
journey.quote: If you are marrying in your own church, temple or synagogue, this is usually the category that applies.
journey.reaction: Our family would want our own faith in the ceremony, and this list leaves out a mosque. I can't tell from the page whether that's on purpose or just careless. I noticed it.

journey.quote: A registry wedding suits couples who want the legal marriage done simply, often ahead of a larger celebration elsewhere.
journey.reaction: That's what we'd most likely do. Legal part done quietly, the real wedding elsewhere. It's nice to see it described as normal.

journey.section: Can a friend or family member marry you?
journey.quote: Timing is the part couples underestimate.
journey.reaction: This is the one section that actually changes a conversation at home. Up to six months, no fast-tracking, and you need to start well over a year out. Clear, and it saves an awkward discussion with my father's friend.

journey.section: Can a friend or family member marry you?
journey.reaction: Sensible advice, and it's said without fuss. A reading or a welcome from the family friend is the obvious answer.

journey.section: What your celebrant must do to make it legal
journey.quote: Your celebrant must meet separately and in person with each of you before the marriage is solemnised.
journey.reaction: That matters for us because I'm in Dubai. Where does that meeting happen, and can it be private? The page says plan early but doesn't go further.

journey.section: What your celebrant must do to make it legal
journey.quote: The celebrant keeps the celebrant copy of the official certificate for six years from the date of the marriage.
journey.reaction: Fine, but our names and details sit with a celebrant and a registry. Nothing here is about privacy, though I accept that's the law and not the brand.

journey.section: Who can marry you if your wedding is overseas?
journey.quote: Not your Australian celebrant, at least not legally.
journey.reaction: Direct. I like an answer in the first line. The two paths that follow are exactly the decision our family has to make.

journey.section: Who can marry you if your wedding is overseas?
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments for the celebration abroad as your single point of contact, in your time zone and quoting in AUD, while the legal ceremony stays with you and your celebrant: speak with [Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=who-can-perform-a-marriage&utm_content=secondary).
journey.reaction: Honest about where their job ends, which I respect. But it's written for a couple watching their budget. Nothing on guest numbers, exclusive use or discretion. One advisor for 300 guests across three countries? I'd want to know who's behind them.

journey.quote: Once you know who will marry you, and where the legal ceremony happens, the rest is the part your guests will remember.
journey.reaction: Warm without being eager. A good line.

journey.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, anywhere in the world, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: 'Anywhere in the world' suits a family across Dubai, Sydney and London. Leading with the fee being agreed upfront feels like reassurance for someone afraid of being overcharged. That isn't my worry.

unanswered_questions: Can the separate in-person celebrant meetings happen privately, and where, if one of us lives in Dubai?
Can a registry or small legal ceremony in Sydney be held privately, for example at a family home, with only close family?
Who holds our personal details and certificates after the legal ceremony, and how are they kept?
Have they planned a celebration abroad for 200 to 400 guests, with exclusive use and our own security working alongside the venue's?
Can they accommodate an Islamic or mixed-faith element within a celebration abroad, and do they work with officiants from our own community?
Does one Wedded Advisor work alone, or is there a team behind them at our scale?
Is there a private or referral route to someone senior, rather than the Wedded Concierge web page?

turn_offs_found.quote: The two Commonwealth types share one regulator and one register, which is why they are sometimes grouped as a single type, with three groups in all.
turn_offs_found.why: This is over-explaining. Four types, then three groups, then 'either way, the same people'. It wastes my assistant's time and makes the page read like a textbook rather than a firm that knows what matters.

turn_offs_found.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, anywhere in the world, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
turn_offs_found.why: Putting the fee up front reads as value reassurance, which is the language of a standard client. I don't want to be sold on 'no surprises'. I want to know what's possible.

would_share_with: My father, for the 'Can a friend or family member marry you?' section, since he wants a family friend to officiate
My assistant and family office, for the register check steps and the overseas two-path choice

cta_reaction.why: The tone is quiet and they're honest about not handling the law, which I respect. But nothing speaks to scale or discretion, and the close is pitched at a couple worried about fees. I wouldn't fill in a web form. If someone we trust referred them, my assistant would make the call.

top_3_changes: In 'Ministers of religion from a recognised denomination', change 'your own church, temple or synagogue' to wording that doesn't name only some faiths, such as 'your own place of worship', so readers of other faiths don't feel left out.

Cut the sentence 'The two Commonwealth types share one regulator and one register, which is why they are sometimes grouped as a single type, with three groups in all.' and the 'Either way' line after it. The section is clearer with four types stated once.

In the Wedded Advisor paragraph or the closing paragraph, add one line inviting couples with large guest lists, several faiths or privacy needs to say so when they first get in touch. That acknowledges scale and discretion without claiming capabilities the page can't support.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction quotes the exact sentence from 05-draft.md
Stayed in character as Layla (UHNW, Dubai with family in Sydney and London; assistant reads first; cares about discretion, scale, cultural awareness, not being treated as a package client)
No invented brand facts; capability gaps listed as unanswered questions
Ignored HTML comments, image slots and VERIFY markers
Journey types limited to gained_trust, lost_trust, confused, bored, excited, objection; every turn-off has a why
Deferred business details and transfers not treated as must-fix; absent prices and celebrant names accepted by design; no request for sourcing

assumptions: Layla's family is considering a family friend as officiant and has not yet chosen between a legal ceremony in Sydney and marrying legally abroad.
Her family is Muslim or of mixed faith, consistent with the card's Dubai base and focus on cultural awareness; the card does not state her religion.
Her assistant read first and summarised, per decision_behaviour, within a 5-minute budget.
Guest count of about 300, within the card's 200 to 400.
